lead: A continuous beam runs over three or more supports. The bending moments at its supports are unknown, so equilibrium alone cannot find them. Clapeyron's three-moment equation links the moments at three consecutive supports in one line. Write it for each pair of spans and you get simultaneous equations for the whole beam. Aircraft floor beams, engine mounts and wing spar splices often use such continuous runs. Only a few universities teach this equation; most now prefer moment distribution (see 2.8).
prereq: You need: 2.6 for releasing a redundant and Unit 1 for free bending moment diagrams.

blocks.text: Take three consecutive supports A, B, C. Span AB = L₁ and span BC = L₂, in metres. M_A, M_B, M_C are the support moments, in kN·m. Use sagging positive and hogging negative. The free bending moment diagram is what the span would carry if it were a simple beam.
M_A L₁ + 2M_B(L₁ + L₂) + M_C L₂ = −6(A₁x̄₁/L₁ + A₂x̄₂/L₂)
blocks.where: A₁, A₂ are the areas of the free bending moment diagrams of the two spans, in kN·m²; x̄₁, x̄₂ are the distances of their centroids from the outer supports A and C, in metres.

blocks.text: The right side is negative for downward loads. A simply supported end has M = 0; a fixed end has M unknown and needs one more equation.
Two load cases cover most questions. For a uniform load w₁ on L₁ and w₂ on L₂, the right side becomes

blocks.where: w₁, w₂ are the uniform loads in kN/m on the two spans.

blocks.where: P₁, P₂ are the point loads in kN at midspan of the two spans.

items: Write the equation for each set of three consecutive supports.
Put M = 0 at every simple end.
Keep M unknown at every fixed or continuous support.
Substitute the free-diagram area and centroid distance.
Solve the simultaneous equations for the unknown support moments.

blocks.text: Measure x̄₁ from A and x̄₂ from C, not from B. A fixed end adds an unknown M; solve it with an extra condition or by releasing a redundant as in 2.6.

examples.question: A continuous beam has two spans, AB = 6 m and BC = 4 m, with simple supports at A and C and a continuous support at B. A uniformly distributed load w = 10 kN/m acts on both spans. Find the bending moment at B.
steps: L₁ = 6 m, L₂ = 4 m, w = 10 kN/m. Simple ends give M_A = 0 and M_C = 0.
For a simple span under UDL, A = wL³/12 and 6Ax̄/L = wL³/4. For AB: 10 × 6³ / 4 = 540 kN·m². For BC: 10 × 4³ / 4 = 160 kN·m².
examples.answer: M_B = −35 kN·m, a hogging moment at support B.

traps: Losing the sign: a hogging moment at an intermediate support is negative when sagging is positive.
Measuring x̄ from B instead of the outer support A or C.
Forgetting that a simple end has M = 0 but a fixed end has an unknown M.
Using the total beam length instead of each span length separately.

quiz.q: State Clapeyron's three-moment equation for spans L₁ and L₂.
quiz.a: M_A L₁ + 2M_B(L₁ + L₂) + M_C L₂ = −6(A₁x̄₁/L₁ + A₂x̄₂/L₂).

quiz.q: Why does a simply supported end simplify the equation?
quiz.a: Its support moment is zero, so one unknown and its term disappear.

quiz.q: Two simple-ended spans, 5 m and 3 m, carry UDL 8 kN/m on both. Find M_B.
A fixed end at A changes what in the equation?
quiz.a: M_A is no longer zero. It stays unknown and needs an extra compatibility condition or a released redundant.

quiz.q: For a central point load P on one simple span L, what is the right-side term?
Why is the centroid measured from the outer support?
quiz.a: The derivation takes moments of the free bending moment diagram about the outer supports A and C, so x̄₁ is from A and x̄₂ is from C.

beyond: Not for the exam. Commercial frame analysis software builds the same equations in matrix form for hundreds of supports. Settlement, temperature and varying EI add terms that this unit leaves out. Searching 'three-moment equation settlement' or 'Clapeyron theorem continuous beam' leads to those extensions.
